strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations in EEG tokenization: non-discrete representations, frequency collapse, and poor scalability
Solid technical approach combining STFT and raw signal patches with thoughtful design choices (e.g., gated patchwise aggregation, removal of positional encodings for non-stationary EEG)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 diverse EEG datasets with consistent improvements (5% balanced accuracy, 9% Cohen's Kappa on TUEV) and 3x parameter reduction
Excellent analysis of learned token quality including novel class-token uniqueness metric, spectral entropy validation, retrieval experiments, and visual interpretability (Figure 5)
Thorough ablation studies validating joint frequency-temporal modeling, masking strategies, vocabulary size, and position embeddings
Strong reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, STFT configurations, proper dataset splits, and five random seeds with std. dev.
Demonstrates ability to enhance existing foundation models (LaBraM integration showing 9% balanced accuracy improvement)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines established components (VQ-VAE, STFT, transformers, masking) for EEG application rather than introducing novel algorithms

Critical gap between motivation and evaluation: claims about generalization and scalability across diverse EEG settings are not experimentally validated—all experiments use single-dataset settings (pretrain and finetune on same dataset)
No cross-dataset generalization experiments despite being core motivation; no evidence that approach works across different channel configurations, missing channels, or variable-channel scenarios

Unresolved fixed-windowing limitation: paper acknowledges that patterns split across windows receive separate tokens but offers no solution, affecting interpretability and potentially performance on variable-duration events
Comparison fairness concerns: uses different preprocessing than LaBraM (16-channel vs. 23-channel montage), making it unclear if improvements stem from tokenization or data pipeline differences
Incomplete interpretability validation: visual inspection limited to 2 classes with 3 examples; lacks systematic mapping between learned tokens and known neurophysiological patterns
Missing computational analysis: no comparison of training time, inference speed, or memory footprint despite clinical deployment implications
Statistical rigor limited: no significance testing (e.g., t-tests); some improvements near error margins (TUAB AUC-PR in Table 1); multiple comparisons without correction
Insufficient sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter choices (masking ratio, transformer depths, frequency band size) despite apparent arbitrariness
Incomplete scalability demonstration: single-channel design is theoretically scalable but lacks experimental validation on variable-channel inputs, sparse configurations, or missing channels

strengths: Well-articulated motivation addressing concrete limitations of existing EEG foundation models (inappropriate tokenization, insufficient frequency representation, scalability)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four EEG datasets with consistent improvements over strong baselines (BIOT, LaBraM) and thorough ablation studies
Detailed token quality analysis beyond accuracy metrics, including token utilization, class-distinctiveness, frequency learning (spectral entropy), and interpretability
Significant parameter efficiency: 1.9M vs 5.8M (LaBraM) and 3.2M (BIOT) with superior performance
Demonstrates that TFM-Tokenizer enhances existing foundation models (LaBraM) when used as replacement tokenizer
Joint frequency-temporal modeling is well-motivated and ablation (Q1.2) demonstrates necessity across different EEG tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VQ-VAE for tokenization, masked prediction pretraining, and time-frequency analysis are all established techniques; contribution is primarily adaptation to EEG rather than methodological innovation

Single-channel design claim is poorly justified: the method still tokenizes each channel independently and concatenates (Problem Statement 2); no evidence that single-channel design generalizes better across different channel configurations; no empirical comparison between single-channel vs. multi-channel tokenization approaches

Single-dataset experimental protocol severely undermines claims about foundation models and generalization: all experiments (tokenizer pretraining → encoder pretraining → fine-tuning) occur within the same dataset; no cross-dataset transfer, zero-shot, or few-shot evaluation despite foundation model positioning

Baseline comparison concerns: different channel configurations vs. LaBraM (16 vs. 23), some performance improvements fall within standard deviation ranges, no statistical significance tests (t-tests), unclear if baselines received equivalent hyperparameter tuning

Interpretability claims overstated: Q4 uses only visual inspection on 2 classes with 3 examples each; authors acknowledge critical flaw that patterns split across windows receive different tokens; no quantitative interpretability metrics

Frequency learning analysis is indirect: spectral entropy of token sequences is a circular measure (frequency encoder designed to produce high entropy); no reconstruction visualizations or analysis of which frequency bands are preserved

Masking strategy lacks principled motivation: frequency band + temporal masking introduced without clear justification; ablation shows symmetric masking is needed to fix temporal masking issues, suggesting the approach is not well-motivated

Vocabulary size sensitivity: Figure 7 shows no monotonic trend; method appears sensitive to vocabulary size of 8,192 (chosen to match LaBraM); limited guidance on setting this hyperparameter for new applications
Missing critical comparisons: no computational cost analysis (inference speed, memory, training time), no breakdown by EEG event type/frequency band, limited failure mode analysis
Untested architecture design choices: number of transformer layers (2), localized spectral window encoder design, and gated aggregation mechanism lack ablations or justification

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement addressing three real limitations of existing EEG foundation models: lack of discrete tokenization, frequency collapse, and poor single-channel scalability
Thoughtful methodological design combining time-frequency joint modeling through frequency patch encoding, gated aggregation, and temporal transformers with principled masking strategy

Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 diverse EEG datasets with consistent improvements (5% balanced accuracy, 9% Cohen's Kappa over BIOT), while achieving 3× parameter reduction compared to LaBraM
Rigorous ablation studies systematically validating design choices (Q1.2 on joint modeling, Q2 on token quality with multiple metrics, ablations on vocabulary size, masking, positional encoding)

Strong interpretability analysis combining token quality metrics (utilization, class-uniqueness, spectral entropy) with visual inspection showing tokens capture task-specific, class-distinctive EEG patterns
Solid reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, STFT specifications, dataset splits clearly documented, and results reported over 5 random seeds with mean and standard deviation
Practical advantages of single-channel tokenization demonstrated through applicability to LaBraM enhancement and scalability across varying channel configurations
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: core contribution is primarily VQ-VAE application to EEG with straightforward modifications; temporal and frequency encoders use standard components without principled EEG-specific design innovations

Single-dataset training paradigm significantly constrains claims about generalization and cross-task transfer; true foundation models should demonstrate cross-dataset applicability, weakening the foundation model framing
Incomplete analysis of contradictory findings: TFM-Token-R outperforms TFM-Token-S on TUAB but underperforms on TUEV (Table 1), yet underlying reasons remain unexplored

Acknowledged limitations remain unaddressed: fixed windowing can split EEG patterns across adjacent windows causing spurious tokenization (Section 5.5), affecting real-world performance but relegated to future work
Absence of formal statistical significance testing: while standard deviations reported, no t-tests or confidence intervals provided; some improvements overlap with variance bounds
Missing error analysis and failure mode investigation: no characterization of what EEG patterns the method struggles with, no confusion matrices, and no per-class performance breakdown

Counterintuitive design finding (positional encoding removal improves 4% Cohen's Kappa) lacks principled investigation, suggesting possible suboptimality in baseline design that warrants deeper analysis
Limited computational cost analysis: while parameter count reduced, actual inference time, memory footprint, and STFT computation overhead during training/inference not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation that clearly identifies gaps in existing EEG tokenization approaches (segment-based without learned vocabulary, discarding tokens at inference)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four diverse datasets with both single- and multi-dataset pretraining, systematic ablation studies, and cross-device scalability validation on ear-EEG
Consistent empirical improvements across all benchmarks (up to 17% Cohen's Kappa on TUEV) with superior parameter efficiency (1.9M vs 5.8M for LaBraM)
Model-agnostic design successfully integrates with existing foundation models (BIOT, LaBraM) as plug-and-play component, improving performance in 93% of cases
Rigorous token quality analysis including class-token uniqueness, consistency metrics via retrieval experiments, and frequency learning analysis using spectral entropy
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters provided, systematic hyperparameter tuning methodology documented, code promised to be released
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (STFT, VQ-VAE, masked language modeling) without novel methodological or theoretical contributions; core contribution is engineering-level combination rather than conceptual advance

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: LaBraM reproduced with 4 datasets vs. original 2500+ hours pretraining; BIOT reproduced rather than official; EEGPT uses mixed published/author results—making it difficult to isolate tokenization's contribution from training setup differences

Single-channel tokenization design insufficiently justified: device-agnosticism claim could also follow from multi-channel aggregation post-tokenization; ear-EEG validation limited (120 recordings, ~8K samples, 4 channels); no comparison to multi-channel tokenization approaches

Shallow analysis of what tokens actually learn: class-token uniqueness scores extremely low (2.14% TUEV, 1.429% IIIC) with no interpretation of what constitutes 'good' scores; only 6 qualitative examples; authors acknowledge windowing causes pattern splits but don't address it; frequency learning evaluated indirectly

Incomplete masking strategy justification: Table 12 shows temporal masking decreases Cohen's Kappa/F1, with symmetric masking mysteriously recovering performance—no clear explanation for this interaction or training instability

Multiple design choices lack theoretical grounding: why VQ-VAE over other quantization methods; why removing positional embeddings helps (explanation is hand-wavy); vocabulary size ablation shows no monotonic trend with no interpretation; joint modeling validated only by ablation
Modest improvements from foundation model integration: ~4% gains with BIOT/LaBraM (Figure 3) much smaller than standalone improvements, suggesting benefits may plateau with model complexity

Limited cross-domain generalization validation: ear-EEG experiment uses same task as pretraining; true out-of-domain transfer to different modalities/tasks not tested; missing comparisons to alternative time-frequency representations and quantization schemes

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across four diverse EEG datasets with both single and multi-dataset pretraining settings
Well-motivated problem formulation identifying gap in existing foundation models' tokenization approaches
Extensive ablation studies and thorough experimental details supporting reproducibility
Consistent empirical improvements across datasets with notably better parameter efficiency (1.9M vs. 5.8-8.6M parameters)
Cross-device evaluation on ear-EEG demonstrates generalization to non-standard recording devices
Thoughtful integration of time-frequency analysis and single-channel design for practical applicability
weaknesses: Critical issue with baseline comparisons: LaBraM retrained on 4 datasets vs. original 2,500 hours, and BIOT* also reproduced with authors' hyperparameter tuning, making it unclear whether improvements come from tokenization or favorable tuning conditions
Limited architectural novelty: components (spectral patching, transformers, gated aggregation, VQ-VAE) are established techniques combined in relatively straightforward ways

Fundamental value proposition of discrete tokens never convincingly established—no direct comparison against continuous embeddings from same frequency encoder, and integration gains with foundation models are modest (3-4%)
Weak justification for discrete tokenization in EEG: analogy to NLP is insufficiently argued given EEG's continuous physiological nature and lack of discrete semantic structure

Token quality analysis is circular and inadequate: class-token uniqueness is self-referential, retrieval consistency uses crude Jaccard similarity (authors admit 'further work needed'), qualitative analysis shows only anecdotal examples without clinical validation

Overstated scalability claims: 'device-agnostic' is a design choice (single-channel processing) not inherent to tokenization; cross-device scalability claimed from single ear-EEG dataset (120 recordings) insufficient for broad generalization
Design choices lack principled justification: removing positional embeddings improves performance (Table 10), contradicting the motif-localization hypothesis and suggesting improper temporal modeling

Experimental confounds: hyperparameter optimization bias, architecture mismatch between TFM-Tokenizer (lightweight 0.7M transformer) and baselines, missing ablation comparing alternative tokenizers with same downstream model
High token vocabulary utilization redundancy: 8192 vocabulary with only 9.78% utilization (Table 6) suggests potential memorization rather than motif learning

Limited generalization: evaluation restricted to clinical EEG only (event classification, seizure detection); no validation on research paradigms, non-clinical populations, or diverse downstream tasks

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear identification of three key challenges in EEG tokenization (target, resolution, learning objective)

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 4 diverse EEG datasets with both single and multi-dataset pretraining, demonstrating consistent improvements (17% on TUEV, 36% on IIIC Seizure)
Thoughtfully designed dual-path time-frequency architecture with principled design choices (e.g., gated aggregation for frequency, omitted positional encoding for non-stationary EEG)
Strong practical utility demonstrated through plug-and-play integration with existing foundation models (BIOT, LaBraM) showing improvements in 93% of cases
Extensive ablations and analyses including token quality metrics (uniqueness, consistency), frequency learning capability, and cross-dataset generalization studies
Cross-device scalability validation on ear-EEG dataset using electrodes outside standard 10-20 system (14% improvement over baselines)
High reproducibility commitment with detailed hyperparameters, experimental setup, multiple random seeds, and promised code release
weaknesses: Baseline comparison fairness concerns: LaBraM reproduction uses same 4-dataset corpus while original uses 2,500+ hours pretraining; IIIC Seizure re-evaluation details sparse; missing simpler baseline comparisons (k-means, random partitioning)

Limited cross-dataset generalization evidence: generalization within 4-dataset corpus is shown but only one out-of-distribution dataset (ear-EEG) tested; claims about device-agnosticism need validation on more diverse modalities
Moderate technical novelty: core components are standard (CNNs, transformers, VQ-VAE, gating mechanisms); contribution is primarily architectural combination rather than algorithmic innovation

Token quality evaluation metrics lack rigor: class-token uniqueness metric is somewhat artificial and not validated against downstream performance; Jaccard similarity acknowledged as 'initial feasibility'
Incomplete computational analysis: no inference time, memory, or training efficiency comparisons vs. baselines; tokenizer overhead not quantified despite practical deployment relevance

Scalability claims require nuance: single-channel independence is per-channel only; multi-channel EEG still requires flattening and position embeddings; device-agnosticism scope is more limited than initially suggested

Limited EEG domain interpretation: evaluation is primarily empirical; unclear whether learned tokens align with established EEG phenomena (sleep spindles, K-complexes); clinical interpretability not demonstrated

Hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly explored: many hyperparameters present (Tables 13-15) but systematic sensitivity analysis limited; critical choices like frequency patch size and masking ratios lack depth

Limited analysis of failure modes: acknowledged limitations with fixed windowing (patterns split across windows) not thoroughly investigated; only successful examples shown in qualitative analysis (Figure 5)
Some window design choices (1s windows with 0.5s overlap) justified by prior work consistency but not ablated; no comparison of alternative temporal/frequency resolutions
